name: Federal Republic of Yugoslavia
info: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the federation of Serbia and Montenegro formed in 1992 after the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, remembered for sanctions, hyperinflation and the Kosovo War.

facts.capital: Belgrade, capital of the Republic of Serbia and the federation's only city of significant size
facts.founder: The republics of Serbia and Montenegro, by the constitution of 27 April 1992; Slobodan Milošević dominated its politics
facts.predecessor: The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia
facts.successor: The State Union of Serbia and Montenegro (2003), dissolved in 2006 into independent Serbia and Montenegro

t: The United Nations did not accept its claim to continue the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia: Security Council Resolution 777 treated it as a new state, and it joined the United Nations only in 2000.
Sanctions imposed during the Yugoslav Wars brought hyperinflation of the Yugoslav dinar between 1992 and 1994, reaching 313 million percent, the third worst hyperinflation in history.
The Kosovo War of 1998–1999 and NATO's bombing ended with Kosovo under a United Nations mission, and the Bulldozer Revolution of 2000 removed Slobodan Milošević from power.
dyk: Barred from international competition by sanctions, the FR Yugoslav basketball team returned at the 1995 EuroBasket in Athens and won it at its first tournament, beating Lithuania 96–90 in the final.
ev: The constitution of 27 April establishes the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a federation of Serbia and Montenegro
Under international sanctions the Yugoslav dinar suffers hyperinflation reaching 313 million percent
Slobodan Milošević negotiates the Dayton Agreement, which ends the Yugoslav Wars and lifts the sanctions

sections.foundation:
During the collapse of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia, Montenegro and the Serb rebel-held territories in Croatia agreed on 26 December 1991 to form a new “third Yugoslavia”. Efforts in 1991 to bring the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina into the federation, through talks between Milošević, Bosnia's Serbian Democratic Party and the Bosniak vice-president Adil Zulfikarpašić, ended by late 1991, when Izetbegović planned a referendum on independence and violence broke out between Serbs and Bosniaks.

The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established on 27 April 1992 as a federation of the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro, essentially a rump state with a Serb majority. It claimed to continue the international legal personality and United Nations membership of the old federation, but Security Council Resolution 777 held that the Socialist Federal Republic had ceased to exist, and General Assembly Resolution 47/1 barred the new state from the Assembly's work. The new state abandoned the communist legacy: the red star was removed from the flag, and a coat of arms combining Serbian and Montenegrin elements replaced the communist one.
sections.socioeconomy:
The 1992 census counted 10,394,026 inhabitants: Serbs 62.6%, Albanians 16.5% and Montenegrins 5%, with Hungarians, Yugoslavs, Muslims, Romani, Croats, Bulgarians and others. Most of this diversity lay in the autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina, and the Albanian population was concentrated in Kosovo. Belgrade, with a metropolitan population of 1,574,050, was the only city of significant size. The country covered 102,350 square kilometres, with 199 kilometres of coastline, all of it in Montenegro.

Sanctions imposed during the Yugoslav Wars brought economic collapse. Fuel stations ran out of petrol, foreign assets were seized and average income was halved from $3,000 to $1,500; an estimated 3 million people lived below the poverty line and thousands of young citizens emigrated. From 1992 to 1994 the dinar suffered hyperinflation reaching 313 million percent, and much of the country, including all of Montenegro, used the Deutsche Mark instead. After the Kosovo War the economy was only half its 1990 size. Corruption, a large black market and severe unemployment persisted after 2000, when the new government began market reform and renewed its membership of the International Monetary Fund.
sections.military:
The Army of Yugoslavia (Vojska Jugoslavije, VJ) was formed from the remnants of the Yugoslav People's Army (JNA), with ground, naval, air and air defence forces and civil defence. From 1992 to 1995 the government supported the Croatian and Bosnian Serbs, transferring units of the old JNA to the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Republika Srpska rather than fighting openly. Its own role was then limited, apart from conflicts on the Croatian border such as the Siege of Dubrovnik, and sanctions left its units without oil or munitions.

In Kosovo the Kosovo Liberation Army began attacking Serbian police in 1996, and Milošević sent Yugoslav Army units against the insurgency; open war followed in 1998. Attacks were often directed against civilians. 863,000 Albanian civilians were forcibly expelled between March and June 1999, and of 10,317 civilians killed or missing from 1998 to 2000, 8,676 were Albanians; some 169,824 Serb and Romani civilians fled the province. NATO answered in March 1999 with airstrikes on military targets and infrastructure, without the Security Council's approval, and Resolution 1244 forced the withdrawal of Yugoslav forces from Kosovo.
sections.governance:
The Federal Assembly had two chambers: the Council of Citizens, elected by the people, and the Council of Republics, with equal representation for Serbia and Montenegro. The president, a figurehead elected by the Assembly, could be dismissed for violating the constitution, while the prime minister ran the government. The federation joined the Republic of Serbia, with its autonomous provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija, and the Republic of Montenegro under a cooperative federalism.

Real power lay with Slobodan Milošević and his Socialist Party of Serbia, who ran both republics as an effective dictatorship. The first president, Dobrica Ćosić (1992–1993), was forced out for opposing him, and the federal prime minister Milan Panić, who once told Milošević to “shut up”, was made to resign. Zoran Lilić served until 1997, when Milošević, his last legal term as President of Serbia over, had himself elected federal president. After the disputed election of 2000 Vojislav Koštunica held the office until 2003. In April 1999 the Federal Assembly voted to join the Union State of Russia and Belarus, a decision never acted on.
sections.impact:
The FR Yugoslavia shaped the Yugoslav Wars through its backing of the Serb breakaway states, which it sought to establish as independent Serbian republics with a possible later reintegration. In 1995, after the Croatian Army's Operation Storm and NATO's involvement in the Bosnian War, Milošević took over the negotiating powers of all the Serb secessionist movements. The Dayton Agreement recognised Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina as sovereign states and gave the Serbs institutions within Bosnia.

The Kosovo War left Kosovo an autonomous province of Serbia in name but under a United Nations mission, politically and economically separate. The government estimated $100 billion in damage to infrastructure, and economists at least $29 billion in direct damage from the bombing. Sanctions also cut the country out of sport: it missed the 1992 Summer Olympics and was excluded from international football from 1992 to 1996, though its basketball team won the EuroBasket in 1995, 1997 and 2001 and the world titles of 1998 and 2002. FIFA and UEFA treated it as the only successor of Yugoslavia.
sections.decline:
Military defeats and the collapse of the economy made Milošević and the Socialist Party of Serbia deeply unpopular. In September 2000, amid accusations of electoral fraud, mass protests broke out, and in the Bulldozer Revolution his government was replaced by the Democratic Opposition of Serbia under Vojislav Koštunica. The new government gave up the claim to be the sole successor of the Socialist Federal Republic and joined the United Nations as a new member on 1 November 2000. Milošević was later tried at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia but died in prison in 2006 before his trial ended.

Montenegro had already separated its economy from Serbia's in the Milošević era, with its own central bank and currency. The Belgrade Agreement of March 2002 led to the Constitutional Charter of 4 February 2003, which turned the federation into the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro and retired the name Yugoslavia after 74 years. The charter allowed a referendum on independence after three years: on 21 May 2006, 55.5% of Montenegrin voters chose independence, and Montenegro and Serbia declared it on 3 and 5 June 2006.

summary: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia joined Serbia and Montenegro from 1992 to 2003 after the old federation broke up. Dominated by Slobodan Milošević, it backed the Serb breakaway states in the Yugoslav Wars, suffered sanctions and hyperinflation and fought the Kosovo War, before the Bulldozer Revolution of 2000 and its reconstitution as a state union in 2003.

pointDescs.1992: Serbia and Montenegro form the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 27 April, with an army built from the remnants of the Yugoslav People's Army, but the United Nations refuses its claim to continue the old federation.
pointDescs.1993: Sanctions over the Yugoslav Wars cripple the economy, and the hyperinflation of the dinar reaches 313 million percent.
pointDescs.1995: Milošević negotiates the Dayton Agreement for all the Serb movements; the Yugoslav Wars end and most sanctions are lifted.
pointDescs.1997: Milošević, his terms as President of Serbia over, has himself elected President of Yugoslavia, entrenching the power he already held.
pointDescs.1998: The Kosovo War begins as Yugoslav police and army units fight the Kosovo Liberation Army, and sanctions are renewed.
pointDescs.1999: NATO's bombing campaign and Security Council Resolution 1244 force the withdrawal of Yugoslav forces from Kosovo, which passes under a United Nations mission.
pointDescs.2000: The Bulldozer Revolution removes Milošević; the new government rejoins the International Monetary Fund and enters the United Nations as a new member.
pointDescs.2002: The Belgrade Agreement of March sets out the restructuring of relations between Serbia and Montenegro.
pointDescs.2003: The Constitutional Charter of 4 February turns the federation into the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, retiring the name Yugoslavia.

notes: The saved article is Serbia and Montenegro (the FRY redirects there); it covers 1992-2006, and the profile keeps to 1992-2003.
The article never states the federal capital in so many words; Belgrade is given as capital of the Republic of Serbia and the largest city.
The article dates the new coat of arms to 1993 in one place and 1994 in another; the year is left out.
The article cites no works in its Sources section (empty), so references are [].
The KLA is called a terrorist organisation by the FRY and US governments in the article, and it says the CIA aided in training KLA units; both left out of the profile as contested detail.
